entries.title: Hudson Canyon
paragraphs: Hudson Canyon is the largest submarine canyon on the US Atlantic seaboard and one of the largest in the world: it begins on the outer continental shelf about 100 miles southeast of New York City, runs roughly 350 miles out across the shelf and continental slope, and is up to 7.5 miles wide. Its lower reaches, well beyond this survey tile, reach 2 to 2.5 miles (roughly 3,200-4,000 m) deep.

The canyon is the drowned seaward continuation of the ancestral Hudson River: during past glacial low-sea-level periods the river cut a channel across what is now the continental shelf, and that channel -- the Hudson Shelf Valley -- still runs from near the harbor mouth out to the canyon's head, even though it has not been buried by sediment the way most other shelf valleys on this coast have.

This tile covers the canyon's upper and middle reaches, from the shelf break out to about 1,683 m deep -- steep-walled terrain with rock outcrops, mixed sediments and strong local relief that NOAA and the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council describe as an ecological hotspot for fish, corals and marine mammals, and one of the region's most important commercial and recreational fishing grounds.

entries.title: A proposed sanctuary, not yet designated
paragraphs: NOAA opened the process toward a Hudson Canyon National Marine Sanctuary in June 2022 and, as of this survey, the sanctuary has not been designated -- it remains a formal proposal. NOAA's own sanctuary website describes the effort as being in its early stages, with staff reviewing more than 17,000 public comments gathered during a 2022 scoping period and preparing draft designation documents; no target date for a final rule has been published.

Whatever the final boundary turns out to be, part of Hudson Canyon is already protected today under a different, existing rule: the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council's Frank R. Lautenberg Deep Sea Coral Protection Area, a roughly 38,000 sq mi closure across Mid-Atlantic canyon and slope habitat, bars bottom-tending commercial fishing gear -- trawls, dredges and bottom longlines -- from large parts of the canyon to protect deep-sea coral and sponge habitat from physical damage.

In September 2025, NOAA and partners ran a two-week live-streamed expedition using the ROV Global Explorer to survey Hudson Canyon's coral, sponge and fish communities and collect environmental DNA -- explicitly framed as filling data gaps to support the sanctuary review, not as evidence the sanctuary already exists.

entries.title: The Hudson Shelf Valley and the canyon's head
paragraphs: The Hudson Shelf Valley is the largest single physiographic feature on the mid-Atlantic continental shelf: a roughly 150 km channel that starts near the harbor mouth at about 30 m water depth and runs southeast across the shelf to about 85 m depth, just landward of the canyon head, without ever being buried by later sediment the way most other shelf valleys nearby have been. USGS mapping (multibeam bathymetry, backscatter and seismic profiles) found evidence that the valley in its modern form was carved abruptly, by a single catastrophic glacial-meltwater flood, not gradually by the river alone -- the flood cut 15 m-high banks, built a 120 sq km field of large bedforms, and dumped a delta of sediment onto the outer shelf.

This survey tile's shallowest sounded point, 67.9 m deep at its northwest corner, sits on the outer shelf approaching that transition; published sources place the canyon's actual head -- where the shelf valley funnels over the shelf break and the seafloor begins dropping steeply -- a little further north and east, just outside this tile, around 39.66-39.67 deg N, 72.47-72.48 deg W.

entries.title: Steep walls, hard ground, deep-sea corals
paragraphs: Unlike the soft, muddy plains of the open shelf, canyon walls like this one expose steep rock outcrops and mixed hard sediments, shaped by nutrient-rich currents that sweep along and up the canyon flanks. That combination -- hard substrate plus strong local flow -- is exactly what slow-growing, reef-forming deep-sea corals and sponges need to attach and filter-feed, and it is why NOAA and the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council treat Mid-Atlantic canyon walls as biodiversity hotspots worth protecting from bottom-contact fishing gear.

No public dataset from recent Hudson Canyon survey cruises gives an exact, publishable coral-colony position for a specific scan point, so this marker stands in for that habitat type on a real, steep stretch of wall.

entries.title: Down the axis
paragraphs: Following the canyon floor (its thalweg) southeast from the wall, the seabed drops from about 542 m at the wall to 1,220 m at the upper floor point and on to this tile's single deepest sounding, 1,682.6 m, near its southeast edge -- and the canyon keeps going from there. Published figures put Hudson Canyon's full extent at 2 to 2.5 miles (roughly 3,200-4,000 m) deep before it opens onto the continental rise, more than twice as deep as anything this ~52 x 56 km survey tile reaches.

That mismatch is simply a coverage limit, not a claim about the canyon's true depth: this tile was sized to capture the canyon's upper and middle reaches, where the shelf-to-slope transition and the steepest walls are, rather than its full run to the abyssal plain.
